decision: argenv is a star of OCO: gathered by its constellation, and the way every command line of the commons is declared. It is taken as tad is taken today - a pinned git dependency - and stays published on crates.io; it travels as a rhizcut when Rhizoid can make one.
rejected: Waiting for rhizcuts before using it everywhere (Rhizoid's command line is not yet built); leaving it outside any constellation (it would go on slipping).
why: The author, 2026-11-13: it keeps slipping our radar. It did because it was in no constellation - only an observatory that gathers everything held it - and kept no decisions; the rule about it (every tool declares with argenv, 2026-11-11) lived in OCO's place while argenv itself floated free. Checked the same day: of eight command lines, three are declared with it (snapall, lab-agent, oco-agent) and five are not (ocoeco, tad, the engine, devlab, tone). It is the ecosystem's own principle - declared once, as data, so it cannot drift - applied to how a program is told what to do.

decision: An input says where its values come from, and the contract gains one word for it: asked - known only when the program runs, and the program tells them. Whether a set is declared is read off allowed, as today; a list may have no allowed, and its members are then free, or asked. So: allowed given - declared; asked - one of whatever exists; neither - whatever the type admits. argenv answers one question from the contract - what fits here, given the words so far - calling the program's own function for an asked input and handing it what is already resolved. A program is asked from outside through the environment. Tab in a shell, a blank in a form, help (the question asked of an empty line), man pages and docs are surfaces of that one question; the shell's part is a few lines, the same for every program, made by argenv.
rejected: A separate type for open lists (a type says what a value is, not where it comes from: it would double every type); a three-way source stored beside allowed (two places saying whether a set is closed can disagree, and a rule to keep them agreeing is a part to carry); a shell command named in the declaration, as usage's run= (the program is the one that knows, and a string is not checked by the compiler); a reserved command in the program's own space for asking; generating a script per shell with the candidates baked in (asked values cannot be baked); deciding now whether to emit a usage spec as an adapter (left to what friction shows).
why: One need with three faces (issue 25; an id typed and refused three times in ocoeco's form; ocoeco's own free lists that cannot be declared), and the author's picture of entering: each relation selected, not entered; each stroke choosing what fits the next blank; being on a blank showing what can be entered. Prior art looked at first (research where-values-come-from): the world has come to declared-or-asked too, and asks the program through the environment.

decision: The driver is built in Rust (portable-pty, a vt100 screen model, rmcp for MCP), offered as a command, as scenes in CI, and as an MCP server.
rejected: Adopting a Python MCP server; driving tmux (an extra program between, and a coarser screen); screenshots and vision for terminals (heavy, and text is already there).
why: Whatever ships is Rust; the pieces exist; the Python servers found show the design.

decision: The project is called agent access.
rejected: mcp-oco (names one protocol, not the purpose); agent-bridge (vague); tui-driver (one of its parts).
why: It says the purpose plainly: every tool usable by agents.

decision: lab-agent is delivered by the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor@v1); it keeps only its declaration, build scripts, PKGBUILD, public key and install test.
rejected: Keeping its own copy of the delivery machinery.
why: Its delivery workflows were a near copy of snapall's; copies drift and fixes do not travel.

decision: lab-agent records each wait itself - start, end, what is waited on, the project - and requires both on a waiting submit; a gatherer brings the waits into each project's data.
rejected: Logging waits by hand (it would be skipped); estimating them afterwards.
why: Capture must be unavoidable and cost nothing: the place every wait happens is lab-agent's own wait.

decision: Every process a job starts carries the job's mark in its environment (OCO_AGENT_JOB). When the job ends, overstays, or was left by a run that died, everything carrying its mark is ended - asked to stop first, then made to. Something meant to outlive a job is started as a service, not as its child.
rejected: Process groups (a child can leave its group); a death signal to children (it reaches only the direct child); systemd's control group alone (tests, and machines without it, would have nothing; it still helps where present).
why: Crash-only cleanup must not trust the runner to have lived: a dead run's jobs are found by their mark and cleared before anything else happens. The mark reaches children's children, which nothing else here does.

decision: Work is asked for through the jobs repository as files under oco-agent/jobs - apart from lab-agent's jobs/, so during the switch neither agent takes the other's work. A file's top line says who asked, when and its limits, and counts only at the top. When work was asked comes from the asking, never from when it is read. Drivers' beats are the repository's Actions variables. Only oco-agent-github knows GitHub.
rejected: Taking the moment of reading as the moment of asking; a header read anywhere in the script; a separate metadata file beside each script (two writes, and a window with one but not the other); beats as commits; a second repository for oco-agent's jobs (the same trust and the same token, twice the setup).
why: An agent that was down must not see old work as new: the asking's own time makes such work expire instead of run (the quieter cousin of the 2026-11-11 replay). A header read anywhere is how lab-agent's client lost a line from inside a script. A beat every few minutes as a commit would fill the history with hundreds of meaningless commits a day.

decision: oco-agent is built inside lab-agent's repository (oco-agent/), tested by its CI and kept out of its releases, until it takes over and the repository takes its name.
rejected: A new repository now (the reasoning and the code would live apart, and the history would split).
why: Its design, research and backlog already live here; lab-agent must keep serving while it is proven; tad's Rust version grew the same way.

decision: Each driver - a person or a machine - has a lease of its own, kept alive by its beats: a job starts only while the driver who asked for it is still there. Beats are what is known now, not a history: one fact per driver, a newer beat replacing an older and never the reverse; they are kept apart from the journal, behind their own port, with their own check in the measure.
rejected: One lease for 'the' driver (the first design: a silent AI would have stopped the author's work too); beats as journal entries (hundreds of lines a day that say nothing after the next one).
why: oco-agent coordinates work for any driver; one driver going silent must not stop another's work, and must stop its own. Beats arrive often and only the latest matters, so they are state, where the journal is history.

decision: The redesigned lab-agent is oco-agent: born beside lab-agent, which serves until the switch - as tad's Rust version grew beside the Python one - then lab-agent retires.
rejected: runner (GitHub's word - true, but it says nothing of the voice, the journal or the leases); keeping lab-agent (it names a place, not what it belongs to); renaming in place (the old one must keep serving until the new one is proven).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: it is tied to ocoeco by design. 'agent' is the established word for this role; 'oco-' names its family and its dependency on ocoeco.

decision: lab-agent's core speaks its own language and depends on nothing outside itself (a crate with no input or output); every technology - git and GitHub, ntfy, systemd - is an adapter behind a port the core defines, and its words appear nowhere above it; areas are named for what lab-agent is for; the playbook's guards check it on every change; in-memory adapters run the chaos tests. The journal is declared tad tables queried with SQL, and where they live is itself an adapter; finished work becomes glimpses. The journal's SQL is tad's, and tad's SQL is DuckDB's (tad-engine 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb), as tad's original research decided.
rejected: A core that calls GitHub and git directly (the prototype's way, and the root of the incident's reach); folders named ports and adapters (the playbook: names say what the program is for); the journal as files in a repository with no declaration.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: follow the ideal-project guidelines; the implementation must not rely on GitHub - it is today's adapter, and switching it (to Redis, say) must be a clean replacement; git as a heap of files is a one-off mess when tad is a database and ocoeco makes every action intelligible.

decision: oco-agent is trusted with nothing until it has watched lab-agent: a shadow run reads lab-agent's newest log every ten minutes through oco-agent's rules, keeps its own journal, and alerts urgently when lab-agent starts work oco-agent would have refused. It decides; it never acts.
rejected: Switching to oco-agent at once (proven only on the past); a daily report (a replay storm ran 102 jobs in twenty minutes on 2026-11-11).
why: Rules proven on tests and on one night's log should also hold on the days that follow, before they run anything; and lab-agent is still the one running jobs, so a replay there must be noticed at once.

decision: What happened is spoken back to the repository work was asked through, on a branch of its own (spoken): the journal, and each job's log. It is written only when something changed - the journal at most every ten seconds, a running job's log at most every minute, a finished job's log at once - logs before the journal, so a driver who reads that a job ended finds its log there. Only jobs the running agent did are spoken. A driver anywhere uses standing, log and wait with --via; waiting is a beat, and wait's exit status says how the job ended (0 finished, 1 failed, 124 out of time, 3 expired, 4 parked, 2 not ended yet).
rejected: A second repository for results, as lab-agent has (two places for a driver to look, twice the setup); writing on main (the asking history drowned in reports); writing every change at once (commits by the second); speaking every log in the folder when a runner starts (a burst after each restart).
why: A driver must see how work went from wherever it drives, as with lab-agent's results - but in the one repository it asked through. The history of asking stays readable on main. Writing only on change keeps within GitHub's limits on content creation as well as its hourly budget.

decision: Everything that polls GitHub asks conditionally (ETag), so an unchanged answer costs nothing; oco-agent reads what is left of the hour's budget from every answer and, below 500, takes work in only every 2 minutes, saying so once. Writing - commits, variables - happens only when something changed.
rejected: Polling without conditions (about 480 an hour for intake alone); a fixed slower interval (slow even when the budget is plentiful); a second account or token for the agent (two secrets to keep and rotate, and the token is to be rotated already).
why: The 5,000-an-hour budget is shared by everything on the account; one careless poller can starve land, the client and the pin updater together. lab-agent had learned this; the redesign must carry it over, not lose it.

decision: oco-agent does work through Hands - start, look, stop, clear - whatever actually runs a job (processes on this machine today). A job is claimed in the journal before it starts, and does not start if the claim is refused; its end is written as it happens, and an end that could not be written is kept and written at the next step. Each job says how long it may run and is stopped if it overstays. A run of the agent is numbered by the moment it began, to the millisecond.
rejected: Starting first and writing after (a crash between the two leaves a job run and unrecorded); a counter of runs kept on disk; retrying a job that could not start (it would fail the same way, repeatedly).
why: The replay of 2026-11-11 came from work whose record lived apart from the doing; here nothing starts unrecorded. Deciding needs only that no two runs share a number, so a moment serves where a counter would be more state to keep right.

decision: The lab is watched by a dead man's switch outside GitHub: oco-agent sends its pulse to it (OCO_AGENT_PULSE_URL, or a private file ~/.config/oco-agent/pulse-url) after each healthy turn of its loop, at most every five minutes; when pulses stop the switch alerts the author through ntfy. The watcher workflow stays as a second, probing check where GitHub's schedules fire. Lives since 2026-11-12 09:44 UTC: pulses every five minutes, the check up.
rejected: Trusting GitHub's schedule (it fired not at all); a timer on the lab sending the pulse (blind to an agent that stalls while the machine runs); the lab dispatching the watcher (silent exactly when the lab is down); an outside cron calling the watcher (two moving parts where one does).
why: GitHub's schedules proved unreliable on this account: the watcher had no scheduled run at all, in a private repository and then a public one, and lab-agent's daily gather has run by schedule once in two days, hours late. A pulse from the working loop stops for every failure that matters - the machine, its network, an agent that stalls - and needs no clock of our own.

decision: The lab's watcher is its pulse, received outside by Healthchecks: when the pulse stops, Healthchecks alerts. The GitHub workflow keeps the probe of the whole path, run by hand, and loses its schedule.
rejected: Keeping the schedule as a second watcher (it would look like watching while not watching); a scheduler of our own elsewhere to dispatch the workflow (one more service to watch, where Healthchecks already does it); moving the schedule to another repository (the first move did not help - it is GitHub's clock, not the place).
why: GitHub's schedules are best-effort and drop silently (research the-watcher-that-did-not-watch); a watcher that is silent when it fails is the failure this lab keeps meeting. The pulse is proven, and depends on nothing the lab runs.

decision: lab-agent is redesigned around a journal per job, run-once by construction, the driver's lease with park-on-silence, each job's heartbeat, flows of idempotent steps that resume, a working tree per job and side-by-side by resource, crash-only recovery, a watcher outside the machine, secrets kept out of URLs, and its data flowing through ocoeco - in five stages, each proven by chaos tests before the next (DESIGN.md). Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-ports-names-and-tables: ports and adapters with the playbook's names and guards, and the journal as tad tables queried with SQL.
rejected: Patching the replay and carrying on (the other paths stay open); adopting a durable-execution engine such as Temporal or Restate (a server to run and secure on one machine with no inbound port - lab-agent takes their proven ideas into a small core instead, with git as the record it already has).
sources: temporal-durable-execution, kleppmann-locking, healthchecks, crash-only, k8s-jobs, idempotency-keys
why: The 2026-11-11 incident traced to a foundation laid as a one-off prototype; the author asked for the best the world has learned, with the full picture in mind.

decision: oco-agent takes over the running of jobs step by step, each with a way back (DESIGN.md, The switch): it serves beside lab-agent; its client ships in lab-agent's release; drivers move, the AI first; the watcher probes it; and only when it has a voice of its own does lab-agent's daemon stop. Until then lab-agent's daemon keeps running - it carries the author's notifications and the board pushed to the phone - and is simply no longer asked to run jobs. oco-agent's service keeps the lab awake while it serves.
rejected: Stopping lab-agent's daemon now (the author's notifications and board pushes would stop without a word); moving everything at once (nothing to fall back to); letting the lab sleep when idle (it is set to suspend after an hour: it would take no work and look silent to the watcher).
why: Live work, the author's phone flows, the probes and the shadow all depend on what runs today; each step must be provable and reversible on its own. The daemon's voice was found by reading it before planning to stop it.

decision: Drivers say things to one another (oco-agent say, inbox); what is said is a tad table beside the journal. A driver with a channel on this machine has it carried to their phone through ntfy - urgent words on the urgent topic - and what they answer on their own topic is heard as something they said to everyone. How each job of such a driver ended is said to them once, with its last lines. The topics live in a private file on the machine; a voice that fails rests five minutes.
rejected: Notifications as a thing apart from what drivers say (two mechanisms for one act); telling the author how every job ended (hundreds a day: only a reachable driver's own jobs - others say what matters themselves); trying a failed send again every turn; the board in this step (next: most likely the items in progress in ocoeco's data, not a list of its own).
why: It carries what lab-agent's voice had learned: two channels, so the phone can let urgent ring through; the topics' names are the secret and never leave the machine, so whoever speaks never needs them; a failed send waits, since the server counts by the day. And it is simpler: the author is a driver like any other, so one table and one way serve notifications, replies and talk between drivers.

decision: The watcher runs in this public repository (.github/workflows/watch-the-lab.yml), probes oco-agent instead of lab-agent - asking through the jobs repository as the driver 'watcher' and reading the answer from what oco-agent speaks - and counts any end of a probe as an answer. It keeps only the newest probes. Every GitHub listing oco-agent relies on is read from the git tree, and a listing cut short stops the taking-in instead of passing in silence.
rejected: Keeping the watcher in the private repository and nudging its schedule (no way to see whether GitHub registered it); an outside cron service now (another account to create - kept as the watcher's own guard, see watch-the-watcher); listing with the contents API (silently cut at 1,000).
why: In the private jobs repository GitHub never ran the watcher's schedule (0 scheduled runs, while this account's public repositories ran theirs - the observatory's at 07:10 that morning); a watcher that can stop without anyone noticing is the gap it was built to close. lab-agent is disabled after replaying; oco-agent does the work now. A listing that silently stops at 1,000 caused both replays.

decision: The lab is watched from outside by probing it: a workflow in the jobs repository asks a tiny job every half hour and alerts the urgent channel itself - once - when the lab has not answered for 45 minutes; it says so when the lab answers again, and asks no new probe while one is unanswered. It needs no secret beyond the channels: the probe writes its answer back into the same repository with the lab's own token.
rejected: A timer on the lab sending beats (blind to an agent that stalls while the machine runs); a hosted dead man's switch such as Healthchecks (one more account, and still fed by the lab); a probe every few minutes (noise in the jobs repository, and a long job would look like silence).
why: On 2026-11-11 the agent stalled while the machine was on, and the only alert path ran through the agent. A beat from a timer would have stayed happy through the stall; only work actually done proves the agent takes work (black-box probing). Watching from GitHub keeps the alert independent of the lab.

decision: The first part of a place's id says where it is held. For oco-agent's record that is the machine, written so that it cannot be taken for an owner elsewhere, and the place is named for the program whose record it is: MACHINE.local/oco-agent.
rejected: The user as the first part (it names an owner elsewhere); a setting for what the place is called (the machine and the program are there to be read); an id that says nothing of where the place is held (every other id does).
why: Set right the same day it was made: the mark was first written as USER/MACHINE, read off the surroundings - but across the commons the first part of an id is who holds the place, and until now that was always an owner on GitHub. mll/grig said an owner called mll holds it; that is not so, and there is such a person, with repositories of their own. Looked at before choosing: an observatory keeps what it discovers and gathers, it does not go through an owner's repositories - so the harm was small; the name was still untrue.

decision: oco-agent's record says what it is, in the commons' way: the folder is a place (a mark, written where there is none - whose and which machine read off the surroundings; a mark a person wrote stands) that brings the lens of now, kept beside the mark. The lens is the declaration of the tables itself with what it brings into focus added - one declaration, so it cannot say other than what is kept: what is being done now and for whom, what is asked and not yet begun, what was cut off, who is here. The journal adapter writes both when it opens the folder.
rejected: The lab's tables written into ocoeco's lenses (ocoeco would know oco-agent); a setting for which place this is (whose and which machine are there to be read); a lens kept apart from the declaration (two that can disagree).
why: The record has been tad tables declared in the language a lens declares tables in since 12 November, and nothing read them: ocoeco could look only through lenses built into it. Since 2026-11-13 a place brings its own lens (open-commons-observatory/ocoeco, decision 2026-11-13-a-place-brings-its-lens); tried that day with a mark and a lens put on the lab by hand, what is being done came into focus to the minute, typed by nobody. They are oco-agent's own to write: put there by hand they would be gone with a reinstall.

decision: What oco-agent's record is travels with its rows. The agent speaks its mark beside the journal; and what a repository spoke is kept, on the machine that reads it, with the programs' own data - a folder for each repository, holding the mark that was spoken, the journal, and the declaration and lens the adapter writes. So the copy is that place: it can be stood in and looked through, and is in view from an observatory there. Where no mark was spoken the copy says nothing of what it is.
rejected: A second layout for what is spoken (the copy is laid out as the record is); speaking the declaration and the lens too (the adapter that reads the copy writes them, as on the lab); a copy that names itself for where it is (untrue: it is the lab's record, brought here).
why: The author, 2026-11-13: for looking from somewhere else we have the answer at our fingertips - making somewhere else into somewhere here. Looked at: it was already so. The journal has been spoken row by row since 12 November, and a command told to read through the repository has fetched it into a copy opened by the same adapter. But the copy was a temporary folder named by a process number, thrown away; nothing spoke the mark; and since the adapter began writing a mark from its surroundings, a copy would have named itself for the machine it arrived on. The mark is the one thing that cannot be read off where a place arrives.

decision: A driver speaks with git alone where that is all its workspace lets it do. What a driver needs is to read one repository and to put a file in it. An asking is said as its file under oco-agent/jobs - through GitHub's API where it takes the write, otherwise by a push. The asking is itself a beat: the lab counts it as one when it takes the work in. While a job waits unstarted, its driver says it is still here a third of a lease apart - as a variable where the repository's Actions can be written, otherwise as a small file under oco-agent/beats, pushed - and the lab hears both. What a workspace needs for this is kept here: driver-setup builds the client from this repository, and no token of the lab's is copied into a sandbox.
rejected: The lab's token in the driver's sandbox (it can do far more than a driver needs, a sandbox is not kept, and the new workspace does not let it out); a way around the workspace's own way out (refused there, and not tried); beats as commits for every driver (the reason of 2026-11-12 holds); a branch of its own for beats (one more thing to hear, for what now seldom happens); telling a refusal by the words of the answer (it is told from a spent budget by what GitHub says is left).
why: On 2026-11-15 the driver's workspace changed under it, and the lab's one way in was gone. Looked at before replacing: beats were made variables on 2026-11-12 so that a beat every few minutes would not fill the history with commits. That stands, and variables remain the first way. But an asking already says who asked and when, so the beat written beside every asking said the same thing twice; and a waiting driver beat every minute, though a lease matters only until its job starts. With the asking counted as a beat, and beats said only while a job waits, a driver who speaks with git writes one commit for an asking and almost never one for a beat.

decision: What every job that works on the ecosystem does is said once, in oco-work, which a job sources: a place brought to a new branch, an exact text changed, a thing stood on, an entry made, the Rust of a place checked, a program tried and put back if the job stops, looks kept and compared, a place landed, a release merged, a turn entered. A change to a file is sent as the text that changes, not as the file. A summary too long to be a title stops the job before anything is recorded. From a sandbox, ask sends a job and follows it.
rejected: A program for it (these are a few lines each around tools that exist: ocoeco, land, swap, cargo, gh - and no new Python); leaving each job to say it (it was, some two hundred times); words for what only one job does (a word is for what the next job will do too).
why: The author asks that repeated handwork be automated without waiting, and that tokens be saved. Sign every-job-says-again-what-every-job-does. Each word of oco-work is something that was typed again in job after job through 2026-11-11 to 15, and each of its refusals is something that went otherwise by hand.

decision: A job shows files to the driver who asked, and the driver brings them: shown FILE, a word of oco-work, puts a page or a screenshot made on the lab on the branch shots of the jobs repository; brought NAME, a tool beside ask on the driver's side, fetches it from there by its name. A page made on the lab is then looked at where the driver is - at any width, in the dark, with a fold opened - as often as needed.
rejected: A screenshot for every look (a job and minutes for each, and what is seen is only what was asked for beforehand); another way between the lab and a driver than the jobs repository (it is the one way they already share, and a driver's workspace is let read it); the token named on a command line to fetch with (it is read from where it is kept and handed over out of sight of the list of what runs).
why: On 2026-11-15 six jobs each carried the same eight lines to put screenshots where the driver could fetch them, and the driver fetched each with a line typed again: handwork repeated, and the driver's half of it kept nowhere - on the day a workspace was replaced and what was kept nowhere was lost. And a look took a job each time: one for each width, each part of a long page. The page itself, brought once, shows all of that.

decision: Two things every session did by hand are words of a job. turn ID AFTER AT TEXT [SAID] enters the author's turn as it was said, with the moment it was said, and stops where the conversation's place does not hold with it. settled REPO WORKFLOW waits until none of a workflow's runs is under way and says how the latest ended.
rejected: A wait inside each job that needs one (the same loop, written again, is how one came to watch the wrong run); a turn entered without its moment (when a thing was said is part of what was said).
why: On 2026-11-15 each turn was entered by six lines written again in each job - the word for it carried no moment and went on where the entry failed - and a wait for a harvest or an observing to end was written three times, each a little differently; one of them took a run that had been cancelled for the one that mattered. The lens of results had counted watching a run by hand nine times before that day.

decision: The word released says a release only once it can be taken: after its pull request is merged it waits until the new release is there with its files - as many as the release before it had - and brings the place held to its main, so that a look over the places held sees the release. And a place that takes what is entered straight on its main - the conversation - has a word for it: straight checks, records, commits and pushes the place as it stands, after fresh PLACE main.
rejected: Waiting a fixed time (a release's files take as long as they take); leaving the place held where it stood (what is held is what a look reads: it would go on saying the release had not happened); a pull request for each row the conversation takes (it has no checks of its own to wait for - the check is made before the push, where the row is entered).
why: On 2026-11-15 a job waited for a release's files with a loop written in it, and the next job needed the same loop; a look over the places held said nothing had been released after a release was, for the place held stood where its change had landed, one change behind; and the lens of what followed was kept in the conversation's place by lines written out in the job, as each turn once was. What is written again in each job is a word of a job.

decision: A driver without a terminal has the window through two small things. window, on its own side, carries what it says - a mark, a lens, an entry by its name with what it asks beneath - to the lab, and brings back what is shown. said, a word of a job, says it in the window there and lands what was entered, in the place the window says it was kept in. Neither knows what the words mean.
rejected: A job written out for each look and each entry (what the agent had been doing: the way in remembered from outside); landing left to the driver (an entry kept and not landed is seen by no one else, and holds the place it is in).
why: The author, 2026-11-15: an interface one stands in and acts from, not commands with flags held in one's context. The window is ocoeco's; what a driver elsewhere needs is only that its words are carried there, and that what it enters lands as every change does.

decision: Landing the language's place, where what lands changes the language, is checked with the places beside it: every lens they keep comes into focus with the language as it would land.
rejected: Every landing of the language's place checked with the places beside it (each would take longer, where most change no lens).
why: A change to the language made from the window landed checked in the language's place alone, and stopped the conversation's lens of what followed - seen only at the end of the turn.

decision: A job's trail is its own: what a job stands on says where its work was made, and is no step of the driver who asked for it. It is kept in a trail of the job's, read by the record of its work, and left with the job. The window, said within a job, is the driver's own act: it steps where the driver stands, and what it enters lands with where the driver stood.
rejected: A job standing as a driver of another name (the record of its work would then be by another); where a job worked given to its record in words (where work was made is read off the act of standing, as it is in the window); the driver standing again after each job where they stood before (a step taken to undo a step).
why: A job stood on things to say where its work was made, in the trail of the driver who asked for it: after each job the driver stood in the window where the job had stood, and what was said next was looked through from a thing of the job's. One trail carried two acts - where the driver looks, and where a job says it worked.

decision: Every job says where the language's place is held on the lab, so that every look and check it makes - a place's own check among them - reads the language as its place keeps it.
rejected: Each place made to have the language's place in view (a place's mark says what it is, not where the lab keeps the language).
why: A place is checked where it is held, and from there the language's place is not in view: its check read the language the program carries, older than what had been changed from the window.

decision: Landing the place that keeps the words every job uses puts them to use: where what landed differs from what is in use, it takes its place, and the next job begins with it. The job that landed them goes on with the words it began with.
rejected: The words in use being the place's own file, linked (a job at work in that place would be working with words not yet landed); every job looking, as it begins, whether the words have changed (a look each time, for what changes only when that place lands).
why: A job that changed the words put them to use by a line of its own, each time - until one did not, and a saying was carried by the words from before: half of what it entered stayed unlanded. What is done after every landing of that place belongs to the landing.

decision: What is said in the window may enter more than one thing; the word that carries it lands all that one saying entered in a place as one landing, named by the first and saying how many more.
rejected: One landing for all the places a saying entered in (a landing is a place's own: each place is checked and landed by itself).
why: A sign and the connection that leads from it are one act; landed as two they were two rounds of checks, and a moment in between when one was there without the other.

decision: landit checks a place kept by tad (tables.toml beside its data) with tad alone - tad check, then make verify where its Makefile has it, as its CI does - and commits it without a glimpse; ocoeco check and glimpses stay only for places without tables.toml.
rejected: Keeping ocoeco check beside tad's in tad places (ocoeco's lens would still decide what a tad base may hold); detecting tad places by a missing glimpses export (a tad place may still export to the observatory; tables.toml is what makes it tad's).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: our systems must not depend on ocoeco. landit ran ocoeco check in every place, linux-phone's and ideal-agent's included, so a tad place's own rules were overruled by ocoeco's lens: ideal-agent's about values were refused until ocoeco's reasoning lens was changed (ocoeco #458) - the dependency the author named.

decision: The shared skills of oco-agent/skills (lab-session-start, land-a-change, change-the-phone, record-the-work) and the practices lab-agent guide reads move to grenudi/ideal-agent: the skills ship in its Claude Code plugin (change-the-phone's general part as change-a-device; its devlab part stays in linux-phone-oco), and guide reads the practices live from ideal-agent's database (data/practices.json), its built-in copy refreshed from there. oco-agent/skills keeps only a README pointing there; the lab's ~/.claude/skills links are removed once the plugin's skills are proven.
rejected: Keeping the skills here and linking ideal-agent to them (two homes for one thing); a copy in both places (copies drift).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: one repository, grenudi/ideal-agent, is the one home of general agent know-how (its decision 2026-11-17-one-home-for-agent-know-how). Linked from this clone into one machine's ~/.claude/skills the skills reached no other machine or cloud session; the plugin installs them anywhere. This carries forward 2026-11-17-skills-shared-by-every-agent: procedures kept once, as skills.

decision: The procedures every agent on the lab follows are kept once, as Claude Code skills in oco-agent/skills (lab-session-start, land-a-change, change-the-phone, record-the-work), linked into the lab's ~/.claude/skills so every session finds them when the work calls for them; they point to oco-work's words and carry the traps met.
rejected: Each brief repeating the procedures (copies drift, and a brief is read once at the start); a separate skills repository (one more place for what oco-agent already is - how agents work on the lab).
why: Read in ArtCraft's organisation (craft-skills): procedures shared as agent skills, discoverable rather than remembered. On 2026-11-17 four sessions worked on the lab at once, and the same traps cost time more than once: a clone reset by fresh took unlanded files, docs' rendered pages lagged a row entered after rendering, land merged a release PR from a shell without oco-work.

decision: A tad dataset is DuckDB's EXPORT DATABASE folder - one JSON-lines file per table - edited with SQL and brought back to canonical, diffable files; jq and Miller work on the same files.
rejected: Doltgres and Dolt (history where a pull request cannot show it); gitsheets (no SQL, no joins); GlueSQL (an engine reinvented, without ALTER TABLE); SQLite with sqlite-diffable.
sources: duckdb-spike, tad-origin-log, duckdb-export, dolt, gitsheets, sqlite-diffable
why: Everything queryable, versioned and diffable in one place; measured in the spike: a no-op round trip leaves zero diff at 200,000 rows, one changed row is one changed line.

decision: tad was extracted from a repository that already worked (the software-engineering canon), not designed first in the abstract.
rejected: Designing the template first.
why: An abstraction is right only once it has met a real case; designing first risked assumptions that would not survive real content.

decision: Each repository vendored the engine as a git subrepo at .tad/, pinned in a readable .gitrepo, one commit per sync. Superseded 2026-11-11: copies drifted (three of four older); tad is now called, not copied - released binaries, pinned per repository, moved weekly (2026-11-11-one-release-path, 2026-11-11-pins-moved-by-the-lab).
rejected: git subtree (two commits per sync, the pin buried in a commit trailer).
why: Tested against git subtree on a real update: subrepo writes one commit per sync instead of two and states the pinned commit plainly.

decision: tad is released by release-please (versions and changelog from conventional commits) with the package conveyor building binaries in the same run; the tag-triggered workflow is gone.
rejected: Tagging by hand with land --tag as the release path; keeping both paths.
why: One release path, no manual version bumps; a tag made with GitHub's own token cannot start another workflow, so the binaries are built in the same run.

decision: The lab machine moves each repository's tad pin (bin/update-pins.sh, weekly), landing through land so each repository's CI decides.
rejected: A GitHub workflow with GitHub's token (its pull requests start no CI); the author's personal token as a secret in four repositories (spreads the key); a GitHub App (the clean CI-native way - needs the author's setup; a later upgrade).
why: A pull request opened by a workflow with GitHub's own token starts no CI, so a pure-GitHub updater would open unchecked pull requests; the lab machine already holds a token and lands through checks.

decision: tad in Rust: tables declared as data (after Frictionless Table Schema); one tool - check, canonical form, row edits with a check, documents rendered from data; proven equal to the Python version on all four repositories (same verdicts, same documents) before any switch; delivered by the package conveyor instead of vendored; ocoeco's shapes become a tad declaration. The tool is delivered by the package conveyor (for CI and machines); the library is taken as a Rhizoid cutting where a project builds on it (ocoeco) - as tad's own path already says, a rhizcut in every repository. Corrected 2026-11-12 by 2026-11-12-sql-again: SQL is not optional - tad answers real SQL through an embedded SQLite.
rejected: Rust bindings to DuckDB keeping schema.sql (a database engine to validate text); Dolt (a separate store); keeping the vendored copies.
why: The author: tad stays general and Python leaves. The four schemas need no database engine: their 41 tables use only patterns, allowed values, required fields and one list column.

decision: When the four repositories switch to tad, their documents are re-rendered by today's renderer; the canon's and Rhizoid's change visibly, and that is said in the switch's own change.
rejected: Porting the older renderers too, to switch without visible change.
why: Their vendored copies are older; the switch is the first time they get today's renderer. A change people did not expect should be announced, not discovered.

decision: tad's SQL engine is a port in tad's own words (load the declared tables, run a statement, give the tables back), and its adapter today is DuckDB's pinned standalone binary, checked by fingerprint and installed beside tad; a stand-in serves the tests; an embedded DuckDB stays possible as another adapter if it ever builds statically.
rejected: Embedding DuckDB now (no static build, slow builds, a large binary).
why: Measured (carrying-duckdb): embedding costs six minutes per build, 66 MB, and no static release; the standalone binary is fast, published for both architectures and already trusted by the feeds.

decision: How pages read is declared in tables.toml ([site] and [pages.<table>]) and rendered by tad; no repository keeps a renderer of its own. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-tad-is-text-as-data: presentation stays declared as data, but in the renderer's own file, not in tables.toml, and the renderer leaves tad.
rejected: A renderer per repository (code each must keep, and DuckDB with it in the canon's case).
why: The canon kept its own renderer only for its presentation; declared as data, its seven pages came out identical but for the notice line, and any repository can say how it reads.

decision: tad answers real SQL again: tad sql runs a statement over the declared tables through an embedded SQLite - a query reads them, a change is checked by tad (every row and rule) before the tables are written back in canonical form, as the Python version did with DuckDB. Proven equal on the four repositories' own queries before anyone relies on it. Superseded the same day by 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb: the original 2026-09 research had already weighed SQLite and chosen DuckDB.
rejected: No SQL (the rewrite's choice - it left tad unable to answer questions about its own data); GlueSQL (pure Rust, storage as a trait, but younger and a smaller dialect); DataFusion (built for analytics at scale, heavy for this); DuckDB again (a large engine to embed, and the declaration already gives the types).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the whole point of tad is that it can be used with real SQL; and lab-agent's journal will be tad tables that must be queried. The Rust rewrite had dropped SQL as optional - that was wrong.

decision: tad sql runs on DuckDB, as the original research decided: the declared tables are read into DuckDB, the statement runs, and the tables come back through tad's checks and canonical form; whether DuckDB is embedded in tad or called as its pinned standalone binary (as the phone project's feeds already do) is settled by measuring both on the release build.
rejected: SQLite (weighed in 2026-09, and DuckDB chosen); no SQL (the 2026-11-11 rewrite's mistake).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: SQL was the whole point of tad, researched with prior art before tad existed (why-tad-exists). The 2026-11-12 choice of SQLite contradicted that research, which had weighed SQLite with sqlite-diffable and chosen DuckDB for its native file layout, rich types and measured zero-diff round trip.

decision: tad installs its own SQL engine: tad engine fetches DuckDB's pinned binary for this machine into tad's own folder and checks its fingerprint before unpacking; tad sql uses the one named in TAD_DUCKDB, else tad's own, else one on the PATH. The pin lives in the adapter that owns it and moves with tad's releases.
rejected: A copied install-duckdb script in each repository (copies drift); asking each person to install DuckDB themselves (no pin, no fingerprint).
why: An install script copied into each repository is what drifted before (delivering-tad); the DuckDB adapter owns where its engine comes from.

decision: tad's concern is text as data and nothing else: declare the tables, keep them checked and canonical, and make them easy to create, read, update and delete through files, text tools and SQL. Rendering is a use of the data, so it leaves tad for a small tool of its own that consumes tad, taking the presentation declaration ([site], [pages]) out of tables.toml with it; the four repositories' pages are proven byte-identical before tad drops render. tad grows only where working with the data is inconvenient.
rejected: Keeping rendering in tad (two concerns in one tool, and presentation mixed into the data's declaration); moving it into the observatory's engine (projects would need the observatory to show their own pages).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: rendering, or any other use of the data, is not tad's concern; it was added in the Python days, before there was anywhere else for it. Half of tad's code (1,288 of 2,601 lines) is rendering; ocoeco uses only tad's check. The renderer becomes its own tool, not part of the observatory's engine, because no project may need the observatory to work: a project draws its own pages.

decision: When rendering has left, this repository is renamed tad: it then holds only tad. The names tad-engine and text-as-data-template are artifacts of the vendoring era, when the engine was split out to be copied into each repository - an early, hand-made form of what Rhizoid's cuttings are for. text-as-data-template, which still carries the Python engine, is retired with a pointer once nothing starts from it: a new repository starts with ocoeco init and a tables.toml.
rejected: Keeping both names (they describe how tad used to be copied, not what it is); renaming before rendering leaves (the repository would still hold two concerns).
why: The author, 2026-11-12: tad and tad-engine come from the old era, explored before rhizoid and rhizcut existed; the template mixed rendering in, and the engine was what tad should be. Correction, 2026-11-12: it was said here that no repository was ever made from the template. One was: linux-phone-oco/docs, on 2026-11-04 - found when its release proposed the template's version. The decision stands - a repository made from a template is an independent copy, so retiring the template takes nothing from it - but its reasoning is corrected.

decision: tad's command line is declared with argenv (the commons' own crate) instead of clap: one contract gives the parsing, the help, completions for bash, zsh, fish and nushell, and the man page. A named statement's parameters are read by tad against the statement's own header; set's repeated --key and --set are collected by tad, since argenv keeps the last of a repeated flag that is not a list of known tokens.
rejected: Keeping clap (a second way of declaring a command line in the commons, and no completions for nushell); completions written by hand (they drift from what tad accepts); completing statement names from a list baked into the completion script (each place has its own).
why: The author asked for it on 2026-11-17; and the practice is to build on the commons' own crates first (argenv, tad, ocoeco). argenv gained completion values asked of the program at Tab time (argenv-resolve 0.4) so that statement names come from the place being worked in.

decision: A place keeps the SQL it runs as named statements beside its tables: queries/NAME.sql read, records/NAME.sql write, each with typed parameters declared in its leading comment as they are given on the command line (-- --project string). tad runs them by name - tad query NAME --project x, tad record NAME ... (q and r for short) - writing each value as a SQL literal of its type, never as spliced text. A query that would change a table is refused; what a record writes is kept only if every rule holds, as with tad sql. tad statements lists them, and the shell completions ask it for their names as they complete.
rejected: Queries compiled into tad (each new one would need a release of tad); a second CLI over the same database, such as an 'ocotad' (two tools, one database); keeping SQL as unnamed files run with tad sql --file (no parameters, so values were spliced as text); the verbs run or exec (they do not say whether the data changes), call (a stored procedure's word, and SQL's stored procedures live in the engine, not beside the data), select/insert (SQL's own keywords, narrower than what a statement does), ask/tell (unclear to a reader who knows SQL), get/put (they suggest one row by key, which tad set already is).
why: The author, 2026-11-17, for linux-phone-oco: everything goes through tad in one database, and the SQL that writes it should be named and reviewable where the data is. SQL had been kept as loose files run three ways (feeds by DuckDB directly, derivations by tad sql --file, devlab's filing statement built in Rust), each splicing values into text by hand. A file per statement is a diff in the same change as the work that needs it, with no release of tad.

decision: Starting a bare database is tad's own: tad init DIR writes tables.toml with no table, data/, bin/install-tad.sh pinned to the release of tad that ran it (checked against the release's checksums), .github/workflows/tad.yml (check, canonical, pages fresh) and the pages of the empty declaration, so the check holds from the first commit; it writes nothing where any of those is there. It holds nothing of a domain: the standing tables of a knowledge base, the about link and the named queries are grenudi/ideal-knowledge-base's, which starts from tad init. It replaces text-as-data-template's scaffold, which is retired.
rejected: Keeping the template as the way to start (it still carries the Python engine and a domain's example rows); renaming the template into the knowledge base (it would fold a database's scaffold into a knowledge base - the author's correction); ocoeco init as the start (it writes an ocoeco place's mark and records, not a database; the-repository-is-tad named it before tad could start one); a start with a Makefile (the CI says tad's commands itself, a base adds make if it wants); a GitHub template repository (a copy that drifts, as this one did); init with no DIR meaning here (a command that writes needs its place said - practice 8); writing a Pages layout (how pages look for people is the face's, not the database's - the template's RFC-like style stays in its history).
why: linux-phone-oco/docs decision 2026-11-17-ideal-knowledge-base, accepted by the author on 2026-11-17: tad stays a database and gains a way to start one; the knowledge-base layer goes on top, in its own repository. The template was the scaffold of the vendoring era (a Python .tad/ copied in by git subrepo, three of four copies drifted - 2026-09-22-vendored-as-a-subrepo); since 2026-11-11 tad is called, not copied, so a start needs only the pin and the check. Declared with argenv like every tad command (practice 43): init and its DIR are in contract.rs, so the help, completions and man page say them.

brief: bring-up-a-part gains 'A device from nothing': a way back, a feedback channel, a known-good boot, then mainline; and the one-part-at-a-time swap from an accepted stock image
decision: Taken from linux-phone's upstream item, changed to speak of any device: the order a way back, a feedback channel, a known-good boot (the vendor kernel, or the accepted stock image itself, with our initramfs, read-only), then mainline from the nearest sibling; and when stock is accepted and ours is not, swap one part of ours into the accepted image at a time. The walleye specifics stay in docs.
rejected: The vendor kernel as the only known-good (no MSM8998 sibling had one; the stock image serves); phone words in the general skill (UART stays an example among channels); leaving it in docs (it holds for every device the commons brings up).
why: Its research (14 sources) and the walleye lane's afternoon: mainline images accepted and silent taught nothing; one swap into the stock image found the difference. Every sibling port had a channel or a known-good first.

brief: A domain's layer stays where its knowledge is - docs' agent folder, lanes in their device repos - one brief per role it uses, deltas only, checked by overlay-check
decision: No separate repository: the domain layer is the agent folder of the domain's commons base (linux-phone-oco/docs, ideal-agent-linux-phone-oco/), mirroring ideal-agent's roles - one brief per role card it uses, named for it, beginning with the Role, Name and Also lines - and holding only what the domain adds: its devices, tools, places, queries, order of work. Anything general is named (the card, the skill and its section, the practice's number), never said again. A lane's brief (a device's coordinator, its keeper's device part) moves into that device repository's agent folder with its rows (move-device-rows), from a skeleton device-template ships. The folder's README names the ideal-agent version it was last checked against; scripts/overlay-check (6-word runs, 15%) is run by the patrol and by whoever changes a brief; a general finding goes back as an upstream item to ideal-agent (docs' upstream, as #56 did).
rejected: A separate ideal-agent-linux-phone repository with its own base (a third place to keep in step; the domain's knowledge is docs' and the devices'); a linux-phone Claude plugin depending on ideal-agent (later, if the domain grows skills of its own - today briefs are read by path, and a plugin adds a listing to every session); copying ideal-agent's tree into the domain (it is what went stale); waiting for the device move before trimming (the contradictions act now).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: the domain version keeps ideal-agent's structure, references it for general behaviour and adds only specifics, never copying. Measured: half the folder restates ideal-agent and two briefs now contradict it - a copy goes stale. Others pin a base and hold deltas (plugin dependencies, Helm, Kustomize, Debian); nobody checks restating, so the check is ours.

brief: The method stays agnostic; each harness we run is a subject whose how-to is dated, sourced research, superseded when it moves; nothing is kept for a harness we do not run
decision: Practices, role cards' bodies and skills speak of the method only, and skills keep to the open SKILL.md fields (name, description). Each harness the agents run is a subject of ideal-agent's base (claude-code today; records/subject.sql adds one); what the method uses of it is a research row about that subject - dated, with its sources and the version checked - and one summary on top; when the harness moves, a new row supersedes the old, which leaves the subject's answer and stays findable. A skill points to the harness's subject instead of naming its features. A role card's frontmatter (model, effort, skills) is the harness's reading of the card, its body the method. Only what a skill, role or script uses is kept; a harness we do not run, or a model's ranking, is not tracked. Moved now: the waiting, connector, transcript and session-start specifics out of change-a-device, keep-the-start-light and lab-session-start into claude-code-how-we-use-it.
rejected: A new table for harness notes (research with date, sources and supersedes already does it); a last-reviewed field and a staleness script now (the row's date and the subject's summary-due show age; added if a second harness comes); ruler or rulesync as a generator (Node, ~20 harnesses we do not run); our own generator to AGENTS.md and .agents/skills now (only one harness runs; when a second does, the skills are already portable); tracking models and their rankings (practice 35 says to check what the models are when choosing, not to keep a list).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: ideal-agent stays agent agnostic, so Claude or GPT or Qwen or whatever comes are just specifics on how to do it for the model; a small research on how ideal-agent's base is organised, so that latest records supersede old info or show they are old, point to where it was taken, and we do not housekeep records on the ever-changing LLM industry. Others: open formats for the method, a thin layer per harness, dated reviews.

brief: When a launcher refuses because its run is still closing, the lane coordinator waits a bounded minute or two itself and runs again, at most three times, then tells the top coordinator
decision: keep-a-shared-resource ('A run's end wakes the lane') and the lane-coordinator card: neither the keeper's last message nor the subscription is trusted alone; on a refusal for a run in progress, a bounded wait the coordinator's own harness wakes it from, then run again, at most three tries, then two lines to the top coordinator. How, in Claude Code: claude-code-how-we-use-it.
rejected: Polling the runs every few minutes (turns spent on nothing); trusting the subscription (seen to miss); the keeper ending its own run before messaging (its last message is its run's last act; the app closes the run after it); a longer cron nudge (up to an hour idle).
why: The night of 2026-11-17: the walleye keeper's last message came while its run was still closing; the re-run was refused; the completion wake never came though the run shows succeeded; the lane sat idle about 15 minutes until the top coordinator nudged it, and surya's lane waited the same way.

brief: A lane starts its own sessions through launchers - on-demand tasks the author sets up once - run on any turn, its work written into the base first; subagents stay for short questions
decision: Each lane has launchers: one on-demand stored task per role it starts (keeper, research lead, builder), created once by the author so it keeps his permission mode, with a fixed prompt - the role's head, the brief's path, where its work is read (the queue's top, the lane's open question) and the writes it may make. The lane coordinator writes the work into the base and runs the launcher, on any turn; a launcher runs once at a time, so one keeper per lane holds by itself. Short questions and read-only looks stay subagents within the turn. The role hook reads a role past a scheduled run's wrapper. Written into keep-a-shared-resource ('Starting the lane's sessions') and the lane-coordinator card; the harness's how-to into claude-code-how-we-use-it.
rejected: A standing keeper per lane fed by messages (it grows without end, and renewing it with clear_session asks the author each time); the keeper starting its successor (its turns are messages' turns too, and a stranded keeper starts none); a cron waker as the starter (a scheduled run's own start_session is refused the same way; it stays a nudge); a headless run under systemd-run (not logged in on the lab; not seen, steered or archived); launchers created by a session (no permission mode saved, so runs stop to ask); a new launcher per question (prompts vary; one fixed prompt reading its work from the base keeps the board read off the work).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: research and do something about these pauses, so they do not occur in areas he is not competent in and can be done with proper research instead. Measured: seven cards, 4-40 minutes each, all start refusals on a message's turn. Probed: run_scheduled_task starts a session on such a turn.

brief: ideal-agent owns a neutral start, scripts/agent-env: token, PATH, AGENT_NAME signing, branch and land - sourced before every Bash command; nothing of ocoeco
decision: scripts/agent-env (sh, sourced) gives GH_TOKEN from the lab-agent token, ~/.local/bin and ~/.cargo/bin on PATH, AGENT_NAME as the commits' author and committer (given; else the brief's Name: line, kept by the role hook; else the role; else OCOECO_BY; else agent), LAND_RELEASE=0, OCOECO_BY set to the same name for places still on ocoeco, and branch NAME (fetch, a new branch from origin/main, refused on uncommitted work, nothing cleaned). The SessionStart hook names it in CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, which Claude Code evaluates before every Bash command, so no brief or skill says . oco-work; a job outside Claude Code sources it from the clone. land stays lab-agent's command, reached on PATH.
rejected: Keeping . oco-work in every brief (it carries ocoeco and must be repeated in every shell, since an export does not outlive one Bash call); a copy of oco-work without ocoeco installed into ~/.local/bin by the hook (a second copy to keep, written outside the plugin); fresh's reset and clean (it loses files written before it - the hand-over warned of it); landit (its checks are the place's own CI, which land waits for; a commit and land --no-manual suffice); setting AGENT_NAME from the UserPromptSubmit hook's environment (that hook gets no CLAUDE_ENV_FILE); moving land into ideal-agent now (it is lab-agent's and used by everyone; left as a follow-up).
why: The author (relayed by the coordinator, 2026-11-17): oco-work is used only for its environment, landit and fresh; its ocoeco helpers and the OCOECO_BY name are leftovers he does not want; a small neutral start owned by ideal-agent, keeping places on ocoeco working until they move. Claude Code's hooks docs: CLAUDE_ENV_FILE is given to SessionStart and evaluated before each Bash command; the session id reaches Bash as CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, so the start reads the session's role state.

brief: A lane coordinator subscribes to its launchers' completion at its start and re-runs on the wake; a launched session's last act is two lines to it
decision: keep-a-shared-resource ('Starting the lane's sessions') and the lane-coordinator card: at the lane's start and after its renewal, the lane coordinator subscribes itself to each launcher's completion and re-runs on the wake; the keeper card: its last act, after the hand-over and the lease released, is two lines to its lane coordinator - a backstop where a subscription was lost (one subscriber per task, the newest replacing).
rejected: Polling the runs (a turn spent per look); a cron nudge alone (up to an hour idle); the keeper's last message alone (a keeper that ends abruptly sends none); the subscription alone (a renewed coordinator or another subscriber replaces it).
why: Surya's lane sat idle from 18:16 on 2026-11-17 until the author asked why: a launched run is not its coordinator's child, so its end sent no note. Both lane coordinators subscribed (surya 2, walleye 3 launchers) and the app accepted every one on a message's turn; the first wake is still to be seen.

brief: Agents are named sessions with briefs; their shared state is the projects' data, not a tracker; research runs in parallel, a shared device is queued.
decision: Agents are sessions with a name, a brief and places they own; their shared state is the data the projects already keep - backlog, decisions, research, session logs, measured results - read through ocoeco's lenses, not a tracker of their own. An orchestration session tends the conveyor and the agents: it checks the ways by measuring hand-work, turns every rule it can into a mechanism (a tool's hold on a device, Claude Code command hooks, CI), keeps the face fluent, and starts a research session per hard feature. Research parallelises; changes to one shared device are queued through one session. (First decided for linux-phone-oco in its docs, decision of the same id; its linux-phone parts stay there.)
rejected: A tracker beside ocoeco such as Beads (two records of one work); an always-on watching agent (tokens without end - patrols on a schedule and hooks do it cheaper); one agent per feature implementing in parallel on one device (changes race); an agents-orchestration repository beside lab-agent then (one nature under three names - superseded by ideal-agent, the one home: 2026-11-17-one-home-for-agent-know-how).
why: The author, 2026-11-17, asked for an orchestrating agent, per-feature agents, and the most efficient organisation found by research. Read: the Craft apps' fleet (ownership by subsystem, rules kept once, an oracle gating progress), Gas Town (work state in git, agents as identities), Anthropic (few well-bounded workers, parallel only when independent, about 15 times the tokens), Claude Code (hooks enforce, sessions and schedules run) - the landscape rows photocraft-fleet, gas-town, anthropic-multi-agent, claude-code-agents. The ecosystem already held most of it; what was missing was roles, briefs and enforcement.

brief: ideal-agent follows idealkb 0.4.0: every decision and research has a brief, answers give briefs, the whole on demand.
decision: ideal-agent follows ideal-knowledge-base 0.4.0, whose concept brief-first gives every record a one-line brief and every answer briefs, the whole read only when the task needs it. Its 13 decisions and 4 research rows were given briefs by hand; ask-a-knowledge-base and record-the-work say to read briefs first and to record with --brief; a file opens with its brief, its first paragraph.
rejected: Leaving the old rows to the first-sentence stand-in (they are few and ours; a written brief says what matters, a first sentence only what came first). A practice of its own (the skills every session uses already carry it; the start stays light).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: records - tables and files - should all have a brief summary to begin with, read by default; deeper only when the task needs it - reflected in idealkb, referenced by ideal-agent as its implementation. Measured here: the about answer for housekeeping 1.4 KB by briefs against 5.3 KB whole.

brief: Gmail and Claude Docs are off by default for new sessions; Firecrawl stays on for research; a session that needs one asks the author.
decision: The author turned Gmail and Claude Docs off by default for new sessions; Firecrawl stays on. The skills lab-session-start and keep-the-start-light say so: a session whose task needs Gmail or Claude Docs asks the author, who turns it on for that session from the composer's + menu, Connectors. The next keeper's start is measured with scripts/read-weight to confirm the saving.
rejected: Switching connectors per session from outside, by role (the app offers no such switch: it applies to one session and sets the default for new ones). Turning Firecrawl off too (research sessions need it to look outside the commons). Leaving all on (every session pays for tools it never calls).
why: The author, 2026-11-17. Measured (what-a-started-agent-reads): every session held 73-81k tokens before reading anything, nearly all Claude Code and the tools of every connector it carries - Gmail 31 tools, Claude Docs 8 - while the project's own start was 4-6k; a keeper or a research session uses neither.

brief: A keeper's open question goes to its lane coordinator, who decides what can be undone (research first if needed), records it, tells the keeper, sends two lines up; only named classes reach the author
decision: The lane coordinator is the one decider for its lane. A keeper that cannot decide leaves the resource known-working, files the question in the lane's base, sends it to its lane coordinator and takes the next queue item. The lane coordinator decides a two-way door once the records show the way back; where they do not, one round of a read-only researcher subagent on a lighter model (a second only for what the first left open; a long question is a research-lead session on its own turn); it records research and decision before anyone acts, tells the keeper with the id, sends the top coordinator two lines with the id. Through the top coordinator to the author go only: his hands or witness; writes that cannot be undone or risk the resource's recovery; money; outward actions; permissions, security and agents' settings. The top coordinator does not re-decide a lane's decision unless the author does. Written into keep-a-shared-resource and the keeper, lane-coordinator and coordinator cards.
rejected: Keepers asking the author directly (the lane stalled three times in an afternoon); the top coordinator deciding lane questions (it lacks the lane's records and holds the author's conversation); a research-lead session by default (refused on a message's turn, and long for a flag); treating every device write as the author's (most are two-way doors once the way back is shown); unbounded research (endless searching, Anthropic); acting on a spoken answer before the record (the next session cannot see it).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: decisions like walleye keeper-1's should not pop up and block work, but go to the lane coordinator, who, if he does not know, spawns research, records findings and decision as in our ways, sends a small summary to the top coordinator and tells the asking role; a change to roles after research. Others decide at the lowest level holding the information and escalate early (Bezos, RAPID, SRE, Gas Town); humans keep irreversible, outward, money and security (auto mode, LangGraph).

brief: An expert is a domain written down in its records, not a session kept alive: sessions read the rows, hand over into them, and end.
decision: An expert is a domain written down in its project's data, not a session kept alive. Each hard domain is its rows - research, decisions, backlog, tests, sources - plus one research row per domain, DOMAIN-how-it-stands, that holds the tacit part (dead ends, where experiments live, what never to do again), added to item by item, never rewritten whole. A session takes up a domain by its brief and that domain's rows, and becomes its expert by reading them; it is ended when its part lands, or before its context is compacted, after writing its hand-over into those rows (not into notes outside the repository); the next starts fresh from them. Questions route by the record first: read the domain's rows; if they do not answer, message the domain's live session directly, not through orchestration; with no live session, start a short read-only consult from the rows on a lighter model, and write every answer back as a row. One writer per domain and one hand on a shared device. (First decided for linux-phone-oco in its docs, decision of the same id.)
rejected: Standing expert sessions per domain (idle hours lose the cache, so each question re-reads a thousand-message context at full price; the expertise still vanishes at compaction; their context rots with length). Orchestration as the router of every question (a bottleneck and a game of telephone, and it fills orchestration's own context). Claude Code subagent memory or agent teams as the home (a second store beside the project's database; teams do not survive a resume). A Markdown expert-notes file per domain (a second place for what rows already hold). A vector or memory service such as Letta (outside the commons and opaque to the face). Forking a finished expert's whole session to consult it (kept as an exception for a session a few hours old whose tacit context is not yet written).
why: Measured on the lab: sessions grow to 1000-1800 messages and re-read them every turn; multi-agent work costs about 15 times one agent; one device serialises all bring-up. Outside: compaction loses what only later proves to matter and summaries collapse; long contexts recall worse; relayed questions play telephone; every system that keeps experts across time (Gas Town, Anthropic's harness, Claude Code's agent memory, Letta) keeps the expertise outside the session. The author's aim - knowledge that does not depend on anyone remembering - is the first practice.

brief: ideal-agent follows ideal-knowledge-base by pin; every record names its subject in about, a row of subjects or a backlog item.
decision: ideal-agent follows grenudi/ideal-knowledge-base at 0.1.0, its second follower after linux-phone-oco/docs: idealkb's generic queries (about, next, find, row, recent), records (decision, research, backlog, session-log, source) and the generic parts of AGENTS.md and tables.toml, pinned in idealkb.toml. Every record of the standing tables names its subject in about - a row of the new subjects table (ideal-agent, practices, skills, hooks, organising-agents, keeper, knowledge-base, records) or a backlog item - checked by references rules. ideal-agent's own tables (practices, landscape, subjects, about) and records (practice, practice-shown-in, landscape, backlog-status) stay its own. queries/backlog.sql gives way to next. ocoeco's reasoning lens lets a decision be about a subject (ocoeco #458).
rejected: Keeping its own records and naming them own in idealkb.toml (they differed only by lacking about: following is the point). Keeping the sources' by field (the generic sources table has none; the three values were folded into takes as Made by ...). Subjects as practice ids (44 numbered ids are a poor list of what the know-how is about; a short subjects table says it).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: yes to following it here, offered after idealkb asked (its backlog second-follower). ideal-agent is a single-place tad base, the closest fit to the generic shape; following makes an agent answer here the way it answers in any base (skill ask-a-knowledge-base).

brief: Every role minds what it holds: small outputs, subagents for heavy reading; long-lived roles hand over and restart fresh at 250k, at 150k after a batch or an idle hour.
decision: keep-the-start-light extends to the whole of an agent's context. Hold little while working: name the exact command and limit its output, never a bare --help or a whole table; heavy reading goes to a subagent that returns a summary; skills and connectors only when needed; model and effort by role. Orchestration and the coordinator check how agents are brought up with read-weight on recent transcripts. A long-lived role renews itself: when its context passes 250k tokens, or a batch has landed with over 150k, or before resuming after an idle hour with over 150k, it writes ROLE-how-it-stands in its base (superseding the last), lands it, and says how the fresh session starts - the role brief's first paragraph and that row; the author starts it and archives the old. Applied first to the linux-phone coordinator (docs #195: coordinator.md and coordinator-how-it-stands).
rejected: Relying on Claude Code's automatic compaction (it keeps the session and whatever its summary chose, written nowhere another session reads; none of today's sessions had compacted even at 926k). A new skill or practice beside keep-the-start-light (the same nature - what an agent holds - extended in its place, as the author asked). Renewing on a fixed timer (an idle session costs nothing until it resumes; the cold cache at resumption is what costs). A hand-over in a notes folder outside the base (not read by a fresh session; the role's record is).
why: The author, 2026-11-17: snappy bring-ups and every role aware of its own context; long-lived roles compact what they no longer need into summaries and restart fresh. Measured (long-lived-roles-renewed): the coordinator at 840k tokens after 1,222 turns, re-reading 574M; a fresh one starts at about 83k.

brief: The general hooks are the plugin's: no push to main, no Python, the practices at start - a Rust program built by the plugin; devlab keeps the phone's rule.
decision: The general ways Claude Code can hold are the plugin's hooks (hooks/hooks.json): PreToolUse on Bash refuses git push that reaches main and python/pip (exit 2, the reason given to the agent); SessionStart prints the practices and, where lab-agent is installed, the unread messages. They call ideal-agent, a small Rust program in this repository, declared with argenv; the plugin builds it once per version from the source it carries (scripts/ideal-agent, cargo) into the plugin's own data folder. The command reader and both rules are taken whole, with their tests, from devlab's guard (linux-phone-oco/lab-tools), which keeps only what is its device's: ssh, scp, rsync to a phone outside devlab.
rejected: The rules written in shell (a shell line read by shell is the fragile thing the Rust reader exists to avoid: quotes, sh -c, substitutions, sudo and env wrappers). Python (refused by the very rule). A prebuilt binary downloaded at install, first (needs a release pipeline; kept on the backlog as release-binaries for machines without cargo). Leaving devlab's copy of the rules in place beside the plugin's (two guards saying the same thing, drifting apart; devlab keeps only the phone's rule).
why: linux-phone-oco/lab-tools #36 (2026-11-17) proved the rules live as hooks on the lab, but the push and Python rules are the commons' ways (practices 07 and 21), not a phone's: held in devlab they held only on the lab, and only where devlab was installed. Hooks are the deterministic way to hold a rule (landscape claude-code-agents); a plugin carries them to every machine.

brief: Housekeeping measures what a fresh agent reads per role, against a budget; the patrol measures, the owner simplifies, cutting words is only proposed.
decision: Housekeeping of the start is practice 45-keep-the-start-light and the skill keep-the-start-light, the upkeep of idealkb's summary and dated-research layers. Measured: the start weight per role (scripts/start-weight: the session start, skill descriptions, lab-session-start, AGENTS.md, the agent folder's README, the brief) and the base's fixed questions (idealkb's the-measure). Budget: 32 KB a role or a fifth more than last time; 3 KB a front file; 8 KB a brief; a summary due by idealkb's rule. Who: measuring is a duty of each project's patrol, every run (linux-phone: the linux-phone-patrol scheduled task); over budget it files one backlog item; the owner of the file simplifies. By itself: measure, record, file, write a due summary, mark research superseded; only proposed: removing words from a brief, a front file, a skill or the start, moving files, and any change to a practice. Applied first to ideal-agent's own part: the session start prints the practices without their reasons (22.5 KB to 13.9 KB), the reasons one command away.
rejected: A scheduled task of its own (a second waker looking at the same project beside the patrol: one look, two names - measuring is cheap and fits the patrol's round). Housekeeping writing its own digests of a subject (a second way of making summaries beside idealkb's summary record). Letting it cut text by itself (a cut hides what comes after it, practice 03; words are taken out only by their owner, the practices only by the author). Tokens as the measure (they depend on the model; bytes are what the files are, about four to a token).
